column1: What is the difference between anatomy and physiology?
column2: Anatomy studies body structures and their relationships; physiology studies their functions.

column1: Why must EMTs understand anatomy and physiology?
column2: To recognize abnormal function, identify affected systems, interpret findings and anticipate treatment effects across ages.

column1: Why use standardized anatomical terminology in EMS?
column2: To communicate the location, direction, extent and nature of illness or injury accurately in oral and written reports.

column1: What are the EMT's core clinical responsibilities in this chapter?
column2: Assessment, airway positioning, suction, bag-mask ventilation, CPR/AED, hemorrhage control and authorized medications or monitoring.

column1: What determines an EMT's actual scope of practice?
column2: Applicable laws, training, credentialing, local protocols and medical direction; national models and guidelines inform but do not independently authorize practice.

column1: How do national EMS standards relate to local authorization?
column2: Education standards describe expected knowledge; scope models describe provider levels; guidelines inform protocols. Actual practice depends on law, training, credentialing and medical direction.

column1: Does an advanced provider's presence expand an EMT's scope?
column2: No. Equipment preparation or acquiring a tracing is not the same as performing or interpreting an intervention.
Specialized language used in medicine, enabling communication, education and professional presentation.

column1: What are the three types of medical word parts?
column2: Combining forms, prefixes and suffixes.

column1: What are the two parts of a combining form?
column2: A root (core meaning) and combining vowel (helps join and pronounce word parts).

column1: What is the most common combining vowel?
column2: o; sometimes a, e or i.

column1: How does this chapter display an isolated combining form?
column2: With a trailing hyphen, e.g., cardi/o-. The hyphen and sometimes the vowel are removed when joining parts.

column1: How should an unfamiliar medical word be decoded?
column2: Identify recognizable word parts, combine their meanings and consult a terminology reference when needed.

column2: A sagittal plane divides right and left segments; midsagittal divides equal right and left halves.

column1: What is the textbook recovery-position arm arrangement?
column2: Upper arm tucked under head, lower arm extended; maintain airway access and avoid chest compression.

column1: What must be monitored in lateral recumbent positioning?
column2: Airway, breathing, perfusion and pressure areas; avoid excess pressure on the chest.

column1: What is the chapter's 30-minute recovery-position rule and qualification?
column2: Textbook suggests changing sides after more than 30 minutes to protect lower-arm blood flow; not a universal EMS rule. Do not roll suspected spine injury solely because a timer expired.

column1: What angle defines Fowler’s in this chapter?
column2: 45–60° upper-body elevation.

column1: What angle defines semi-Fowler’s in this chapter?
column2: Less than 45° upper-body elevation.

column1: Why is Trendelenburg no longer recommended for shock?
column2: Abdominal contents can press on diaphragm and impair breathing; may increase intracranial pressure in head injury.

column1: When might temporary leg elevation be considered?
column2: Selected nontraumatic shock or simple fainting situations; limited/transient benefit. Not routine trauma care or Trendelenburg.

column1: How should positioning be selected for dyspnea versus hypoperfusion?
column2: Upright may reduce work of breathing; supine may be better tolerated in hypoperfusion. Reassess and prioritize ventilation/resuscitation as indicated.

column1: What structures make up the musculoskeletal system?
column2: Bones, ligaments, muscles, tendons and other connective tissues.
Upper lateral pelvic bone; its superior margin is the iliac crest.

column1: What is the difference between tendons and ligaments?
column2: Tendons connect muscle to bone; ligaments connect bone to bone and support joints.

column1: Why must the musculoskeletal system be strong, jointed and flexible?
column2: For support/protection, movement and resistance to stress.

column1: What are the four skeletal functions?
column2: Shape, organ protection, movement, mineral storage and blood cell production (last two grouped).

column1: What are the six basic skeletal components?
column2: Skull, spinal column, thorax, pelvis, upper and lower extremities.

column1: What are the four bone shape classifications?
column2: Long, short, flat and irregular.

column1: Which bones form the cranium in the chapter's list?
column2: Occipital, two parietal, two temporal and frontal bones.

column1: How do the inner and outer layers of cranial bone differ?
column2: Thick tough outer layer; thinner more brittle inner layer.

column1: Why can intracranial bleeding or swelling be life-threatening?
column2: Rigid cranium cannot expand, so pressure compresses brain tissue and can cause dysfunction, unresponsiveness or death.

column1: Why can blunt head trauma lacerate the brain internally?
column2: Bony projections and ridges along anterior/inferior inner cranium may injure brain tissue.

column1: How many facial bones are described?
column2: 14: 13 immovable/interlocking and one movable mandible.

column1: What is the largest and strongest facial bone?
column2: Mandible, horseshoe-shaped and movable at its joints.

column1: What are intervertebral disks made of and what do they do?
column2: Tough elastic cartilage with fluid-filled pads between vertebrae; absorb shock and are susceptible to twisting, grinding and improper lifting.

column1: List the spinal divisions and vertebral counts from superior to inferior.
column2: Cervical 7, thoracic 12, lumbar 5, sacral 5 fused, coccygeal 4 fused (33 total).

column1: Which spinal region is described as most prone to injury?
column2: Cervical spine.

column1: What qualification applies to the chapter's lumbar mobility claim?
column2: It calls lumbar spine least mobile but does not substantiate this comparison; do not use it to rule out injury.

column1: What commonly causes lower-back injury according to the chapter?
column2: Muscular injury rather than vertebral injury.

column1: How can spinal cord damage manifest below the injury?
column2: Loss of sensation or movement distal to injury.

column1: Can absence of pain or normal neurologic findings exclude vertebral injury?
column2: No. Assess mechanism, motor/sensory findings and trends; follow protocol-directed spinal motion restriction.

column1: How can high cervical spinal injury affect breathing?
column2: It may impair diaphragm function; assist ventilation if spontaneous breathing is lost or inadequate.

column1: How should a painful or resistant spine be aligned?
column2: Do not force alignment; follow protocol-directed spinal motion restriction.

column1: What are the three parts of the sternum?
column2: Manubrium, body and xiphoid process.

column1: Which organs does the pelvis support or house?
column2: Supports intestines; houses bladder, rectum and internal reproductive organs.

column1: Which structures form the hip joint?
column2: Femoral head and acetabulum.

column1: Which bones form the knee hinge?
column2: Distal femur and proximal tibia; patella protects anteriorly.

column1: Which lower leg bone bears weight?
column2: Tibia, medial/anterior shin bone.

column1: Which bone forms the lateral malleolus?
column2: Distal fibula.

column1: Which bone forms the medial malleolus?
column2: Distal tibia.
Proximal foot bones including calcaneus.

column1: How many metatarsals are in a foot?
column2: Five.

column1: How many phalanges are in a foot?
column2: 14: two in great toe and three in each other toe.
Clavicle and scapula.

column1: Why is the shoulder easily dislocated?
column2: The humeral head sits in a shallow scapular socket, allowing very wide mobility.

column1: Which bones form the elbow joint?
column2: Distal humerus and proximal radius and ulna.

column1: Which forearm bone is lateral in anatomical position?
column2: Radius, thumb side; distal third forms most of wrist joint.

column1: Which forearm bone is medial and palpable along its length?
column2: Ulna, little-finger side.

column1: How many phalanges does each finger and thumb have?
column2: Three per finger and two per thumb.

column1: What are the three joint mobility categories?
column2: Immovable (skull plates), slightly movable (vertebrae), freely movable (hip, elbow, knee).

column1: What structures characterize freely movable joints?
column2: Joint cavity, synovial membrane, articular cartilage and surrounding ligaments.

column1: What are the seven joint movements?
column2: Flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, circumduction, pronation and supination.

column1: What are the six freely movable joint types?
column2: Ball-and-socket, hinge, pivot, gliding, saddle and condyloid.

column1: Which joint type has the widest range of motion?
column2: Ball-and-socket, e.g., shoulder and hip.

column1: What is the appropriate field assessment of a painful or deformed joint?
column2: Describe deformity and distal circulation, sensation and movement; do not demonstrate full painful range.
Loss of continuity in bone structure; fragments may damage nerves, vessels and connective tissue.

column1: Why can a closed fracture cause significant hemorrhage?
column2: Bone is living tissue with a rich blood supply in compact bone, marrow and spongy bone.

column1: How much blood may a fractured femur conceal in the chapter's teaching estimate?
column2: 1,000–2,000 mL; potential severity, not a prediction for an individual patient.

column1: How much blood may a pelvic fracture conceal?
column2: Potentially an entire adult blood volume (about 5 L, or 70–80 mL/kg in the chapter); actual loss varies.

column1: What BLS priorities follow major fracture with suspected hemorrhage?
column2: Hemorrhage control, appropriate splinting, warmth, serial distal neurovascular assessment and timely transport.

column1: What happens to muscle fibers when stimulated by nerve impulses?

column1: How does vasodilation affect resistance and pressure?

column1: How is cardiac muscle similar to skeletal and smooth muscle?

column1: What supplies cardiac muscle with blood?
column2: Coronary arteries; cardiac muscle is sensitive to interruptions in supply.

Breathing a foreign substance into the lungs.
The tubelike structure that leads from the larynx to the lungs.
The smooth muscle bridging the open posterior ends of the C-shaped cartilaginous rings of the trachea.
The two main branches leading from the trachea to the lungs, providing the passageway for air movement. Plural of bronchus.
Small branches of the bronchi.
The air sacs of the lungs. Plural of alveolus.
Thin barrier at the alveolar-capillary interface enabling oxygen diffusion into blood and carbon dioxide diffusion into alveoli.
Substance lining alveoli that reduces surface tension and helps prevent collapse.
The principal organs of respiration.
Innermost layer of the pleura that covers the lung.
The outermost pleural layer that adheres to the chest wall.
The potential space between the parietal and visceral layers of the pleura surrounding the lungs, containing lubricating fluid.
The major muscle of respiration that separates the chest cavity from the abdominal cavity.
The muscles between the ribs.
Infrequent, irregular gasping respirations; not normal breathing. Assess for cardiac arrest and initiate BLS resuscitation when indicated.

column1: What are the four functions of the respiratory system?
column2: Respiration, ventilation, oxygenation/CO₂ removal, and acid–base regulation.

column1: What is the chapter's approximate teaching time for brain cells to begin dying without oxygen?
column2: About 5 minutes; not an intervention delay or a precise survival threshold.

column1: What is the difference between ventilation and respiration?
column2: Ventilation moves air mechanically; respiration exchanges gases across membranes.

column1: Which three mechanisms regulate acid–base balance?
column2: Respiratory system, kidneys and bicarbonate buffer system.

column1: How can faster/deeper breathing compensate for excess acid?
column2: Exhaling more CO₂ reduces acid load.

column1: Where does the upper airway end in this chapter?
column2: At the cricoid cartilage.
Nostrils.

column1: How does the nasal cavity condition inhaled air?
column2: Warms, moistens and filters it over mucous membranes and conchae.

column1: How many conchae are described on the sides of the nasal cavity?
column2: Three bony ridges.

column1: Which three regions make up the pharynx?
column2: Nasopharynx, oropharynx and laryngopharynx.

column1: What can travel into the nasopharynx from the shared pharyngeal opening?
column2: Blood or vomit may travel through the nose or be aspirated.
Air, food and drink.

column1: How does the laryngopharynx route substances?
column2: Air toward larynx, food/liquid toward esophagus.

column1: How does laryngeal cartilage change with age?
column2: It hardens.

column1: Which laryngeal cartilage forms the only complete ring?
column2: Cricoid cartilage, immediately below thyroid cartilage.

column1: What is another name for thyroid cartilage?
column2: Adam's apple.

column1: What is the difference between true and false vocal cords?
column2: True cords are inferior and vibrate to produce sound; false cords are superior vestibular folds.
Inflammation of the larynx/vocal cord region.

column1: How is the airway protected during swallowing?
column2: Epiglottis tips backward over the glottis and vocal cords close.

column1: Why does altered consciousness increase aspiration risk?
column2: Upper airway muscles relax and protective reflexes are impaired, allowing blood, liquids or vomit into lower airway.

column1: How far does the trachea extend in the chapter's description?
column2: From distal larynx to approximately T5.

column1: How many cartilaginous rings reinforce the trachea?
column2: 15–20 C-shaped rings along anterior and lateral walls.

column1: What forms the posterior wall of the trachea?
column2: Flexible ligament and trachealis smooth muscle rather than cartilage; esophagus lies immediately behind it.
Smooth muscle contraction narrows bronchioles and increases airflow resistance.
Smooth muscle relaxation widens bronchioles and decreases airflow resistance.

column1: Where does pulmonary gas exchange occur?
column2: Across the thin alveolar-capillary respiratory membrane.

column1: Why is surfactant important in premature infants and drowning?
column2: It reduces surface tension; deficiency in premature infants or loss in drowning increases collapse risk.

column1: What keeps lungs inflated against chest wall?
column2: Negative pressure in the pleural space between visceral and parietal pleura.

column1: What is the distinction between visceral and parietal pleura?
column2: Visceral covers lung; parietal lines chest wall.
Diaphragm contracts downward and intercostals lift ribs outward, expanding thorax and lowering pressure so air enters.
Diaphragm and intercostals relax; thorax shrinks and air is pushed out by the pressure gradient.

column1: What share of breathing effort is attributed to the diaphragm?
column2: 60–70% in the chapter.

column1: What share of breathing effort is attributed to intercostal muscles?
column2: 30–40% in the chapter.

column1: Which spinal nerve levels supply the phrenic nerve?
What does the phrenic nerve stimulate?
column2: Diaphragm.

column1: Why can a high cervical cord injury require assisted ventilation?
column2: It can disrupt diaphragm control; ventilate when spontaneous breathing is lost or inadequate.

column1: Which direction does oxygen diffuse at the alveolar-capillary interface?
column2: From alveoli to blood/RBCs.

column1: Which direction does CO₂ diffuse at the alveolar-capillary interface?
column2: From blood to alveoli for exhalation.

column1: Which direction does oxygen diffuse at tissue capillaries?
column2: From oxygenated blood into cells.

column1: Which direction does CO₂ diffuse at tissue capillaries?
column2: From cells into blood, which drains through venules and veins.

column1: What two factors determine whether breathing moves enough air?
column2: Respiratory rate and tidal volume; rate alone is insufficient.
Volume of air moved per breath.

column1: What are typical features of adequate breathing?
column2: Adequate rate and depth, regular rhythm, clear breath sounds, effortless work and appropriate chest movement.

column1: What chest movement does the chapter describe for average adult adequate breathing?
column2: Approximately 1 inch outward per breath; not an independent intervention threshold.

column1: What adult respiratory rate range is given in the chapter?
column2: 8–24/min; typical average 12–20/min. Textbook range, not a stand-alone adequacy threshold.

column1: What elderly respiratory rate is given in the chapter?
column2: 20–22/min; textbook reference, not a universal normal or intervention threshold.

column1: What childhood respiratory rate range is given in the chapter?
column2: 18–37/min; assess age and other findings rather than relying on range alone.

column1: What infant respiratory rate range is given in the chapter?
column2: 30–60/min; age-dependent textbook reference, not an intervention threshold.

column1: Which breathing patterns can indicate inadequate ventilation?
column2: Too slow, too fast, irregular, shallow, unequal or absent chest movement.

column1: Which breath sound findings suggest inadequate breathing?
column2: Diminished or absent breath sounds.

column1: Which skin findings may accompany inadequate breathing?
column2: Pallor, cyanosis, cool clammy skin or abnormal mucous membrane color.

column1: Which accessory muscle retractions may occur with inadequate breathing?
column2: Supraclavicular, intercostal, subcostal and neck muscle retractions.
Sign of increased breathing effort, especially in children.
Chest and abdomen move in opposite directions, particularly concerning in infants.
Head rises with inhalation and falls with exhalation; sign of severe respiratory fatigue.
Concerning breathing sound at end of inspiration/start of expiration, reflecting effort to maintain lung inflation.

column1: Why is a falling respiratory rate in a tiring patient concerning?
column2: It may signal respiratory failure rather than improvement.
No; assess for cardiac arrest and initiate BLS resuscitation when indicated.
Hemoglobin oxygen saturation, not ventilation or total tissue oxygen delivery.

column1: What may impair pulse oximeter accuracy?
column2: Motion, low perfusion, temperature, skin pigmentation and carbon monoxide exposure.

column1: Does normal SpO₂ on supplemental oxygen exclude hypoventilation?
column2: No. Assess rate, depth, effort, mental status and trajectory.

column1: How does bag-mask ventilation differ from spontaneous inspiration?
column2: Bag-mask ventilation pushes air in with positive pressure; spontaneous inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure.

column1: Why avoid excessive bag-mask ventilation pressure or volume?
column2: It can reduce venous return, worsen hypotension or injure lungs.

column1: What should an EMT reassess during bag-mask ventilation?
column2: Chest rise, breath sounds, mask seal and perfusion.
System composed of the heart and blood vessels that brings oxygen and nutrients to and takes wastes away from body cells. Also called the cardiovascular system.
The muscular organ that contracts to force blood into circulation through the body.
The two upper chambers of the heart. Plural of atrium.
The two lower chambers of the heart.
Structures within the heart and circulatory system that keep blood flowing in one direction and prevent backflow.
The valve located between the right atrium and the right ventricle that prevents the backflow of blood.
The valve located between the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery that prevents backflow into the ventricle.
The valve located between the left atrium and the left ventricle.
The valve located between the left ventricle and the aorta that prevents blood from backflowing into the ventricle.

The principal veins that carry deoxygenated blood to the heart. Plural of vena cava. The superior vena cava carries blood from the upper body; the inferior vena cava carries blood from the lower body.
Artery that carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle of the heart to the lungs.
Vein that carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium of the heart.
The major artery from the heart.
Blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart.
The smallest branch of an artery, which at its distal end leads into a capillary.
Tiny blood vessel that connects an arteriole to a venule.
The smallest branch of a vein.
Vessel that carries blood toward the heart.
Blood vessels that supply the heart with blood.
One of two major arteries of the neck, which supply the brain and head with blood.
The major artery of the thigh that supplies the groin and leg with blood.
An artery of the foot, which can be felt on the top surface of the foot.
Arteries traveling from calf to foot; pulse palpable posterior to the medial malleolus.
Major arteries of the upper arms.
A major artery of the arm, distal to the elbow joint.
Part of the blood that gives it its color, carries oxygen to body cells, and carries carbon dioxide away from body cells.
The part of the blood that helps the body’s immune system defend against infection.
Blood components essential to clot formation and stopping bleeding (the key-term list incorrectly says formation of blood cells).
The liquid part of the blood.
The wave of blood propelled through the arteries because of the contraction of the left ventricle.
Force exerted by blood on blood vessel walls; influenced by flow and vascular resistance.
The pressure exerted against the walls of the arteries when the left ventricle contracts.
The pressure exerted against the walls of the arteries when the left ventricle is at rest.
The blood pressure or force exerted against the inside of vessel walls; the “push” effect that forces fluid out of a capillary.
Swelling caused by fluid accumulating in the tissues.

The delivery of oxygen and other nutrients to the cells of all organ systems and the elimination of waste products from the cells, which result from the constant adequate circulation of blood through the capillaries.
The inadequate perfusion of cells, tissue, and organs with oxygen and other nutrients, resulting in cell, tissue, and organ dysfunction.
Chemical and physical changes that take place within the cells in the presence of oxygen.
Chemical and physical changes that take place within the cells without the presence of oxygen.

column1: What are the three components of the circulatory system?
column2: Heart, blood vessels and blood.

column1: What are the six functions of the circulatory system?
column2: Cell perfusion, blood transport for gas exchange, blood reservoir, acid–base buffering, immune cell delivery, and clotting/temperature regulation.
Between lungs in thoracic cavity, approximately two-thirds left of midline, apex just above diaphragm.
Double-walled sac enclosing heart with lubricating fluid.
Middle muscular layer of the heart; contracts in response to electrical impulses.

column1: Trace deoxygenated blood from body to lungs.
column2: Venae cavae → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary valve → pulmonary arteries → lungs.

column1: Trace oxygenated blood from lungs to body.
column2: Pulmonary veins → left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta → body.

column1: Which valve separates right atrium from right ventricle?
column2: Tricuspid valve.

column1: Which valve separates left atrium from left ventricle?
column2: Mitral (bicuspid) valve.

column1: Which valve separates right ventricle from pulmonary artery?
column2: Pulmonary valve.

column1: Which valve separates left ventricle from aorta?
column2: Aortic valve.

column1: What is the normal sequence of cardiac conduction?
column2: SA node → internodal pathways → AV node → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers.
Sinoatrial node, the heart's normal pacemaker.
Atrioventricular node, next major conduction structure after internodal pathways.
Atrioventricular bundle conducting impulses toward bundle branches.

column1: Where are the cardiac bundle branches located?
column2: Interventricular septum.
Ventricular myocardium.

column1: What determines whether a blood vessel is an artery or vein?
column2: Direction of blood flow relative to heart, not oxygen content.

column1: Which arteries carry deoxygenated blood in normal postnatal circulation?
column2: Pulmonary arteries.

column1: Which veins carry oxygenated blood in normal postnatal circulation?
column2: Pulmonary veins.

column1: Where does the aorta divide into iliac arteries in the chapter?
column2: Around the level of the navel.
Right and left coronary arteries, including anterior descending branch.
Neck; carotid artery supplies brain/head.
Groin/thigh.

column1: Where is dorsalis pedis pulse assessed?
column2: Top of foot toward big-toe side.

column1: Where is posterior tibial pulse assessed?
column2: Posterior to medial malleolus.

column1: Where is brachial pulse assessed and when is it useful?
column2: Medial upper arm/antecubital region; BP and infant pulse assessment.
Wrist proximal to thumb.

column1: Trace blood through the smallest systemic vessels.
column2: Arteriole → capillary → venule.

column1: What is the structure of capillary walls?
column2: Microscopic single layer of endothelium permitting gas, nutrient and waste exchange.

column1: Why do many veins contain valves?
column2: To prevent backward blood flow.

column1: What does the superior vena cava drain?
column2: Upper body into right atrium.

column1: What does the inferior vena cava drain?
column2: Lower body into right atrium.
Red blood cell; contains hemoglobin for gas transport.
White blood cell; helps defend against infection.
RBC protein that binds oxygen and some carbon dioxide at different sites.

column1: What is the role of clotting factors and platelets?
column2: Form blood clots to stop bleeding.
Blood cells, nutrients, wastes, a small amount of oxygen and a larger amount of carbon dioxide.

column1: What is the function of albumin in plasma?
column2: Helps retain water within blood vessels.
Carotid and femoral.

column1: Which pulses are peripheral in the chapter?
column2: Radial, brachial, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis.

column1: What is an apical pulse and what does it not measure?
column2: Mechanical heart contraction over left chest; does not establish blood volume or pumping effectiveness.

column1: Can an apical pulse persist during severe blood loss?
column2: Yes, even when radial or carotid pulses are weak or absent.

column1: What distinguishes systolic from diastolic pressure?
column2: Systolic during ventricular contraction; diastolic during relaxation. Both are influenced by multiple factors, not isolated measures of pump strength or vessel diameter.

column1: How does high capillary hydrostatic pressure cause edema?
column2: Forces fluid from capillaries into tissues.

column1: Why can pulmonary edema impair respiration?
column2: Fluid between alveoli and capillaries impairs gas diffusion.

column1: What does adequate tissue perfusion deliver and remove?
column2: Delivers oxygen, glucose and other nutrients; removes CO₂ and wastes.

column1: What does oxygen delivery to tissue require besides oxygen saturation?
column2: Adequate blood oxygen content and sufficient blood flow.

column1: What is shock in the context of perfusion?
column2: Inadequate delivery of oxygen/nutrients and removal of wastes due to impaired circulation.
No; assess serial pressure, pulse quality, mentation, skin and breathing.

column1: What approximate percentage of oxygen is carried bound to hemoglobin?
column2: 97% in the chapter; proportions vary with physiology.

column1: What approximate percentage of oxygen is dissolved in plasma?
column2: 3% in the chapter; inadequate to sustain survival alone under ordinary conditions.

column1: What approximate percentage of CO₂ is transported as bicarbonate?
column2: 70%; formed in RBCs with water, circulates in plasma and reverses in lungs.

column1: What approximate percentage of CO₂ is transported bound to hemoglobin?
column2: 23% in the chapter.

column1: What approximate percentage of CO₂ is transported dissolved in plasma?
column2: 7% in the chapter.

column1: What is produced by aerobic metabolism?
column2: Large amounts of energy from glucose with oxygen, plus water, heat and CO₂.

column1: What is produced by anaerobic metabolism?
column2: Much less energy from glucose without adequate oxygen, with acid accumulation.

column1: Why can an anemic or hemorrhaging patient have normal SpO₂ but poor oxygen delivery?
column2: Saturation measures occupied hemoglobin sites, not total hemoglobin or blood flow.

column1: Why can ordinary pulse oximetry be falsely reassuring in carbon monoxide poisoning?
column2: Ordinary oximetry cannot reliably distinguish CO-bound hemoglobin from oxygenated hemoglobin.

column1: Can quietness or screaming establish trauma triage priority?
column2: No. Assess immediate threats objectively; a screaming patient may still be in shock.

column1: In the chapter's penetrating trauma case, what were the measured vital signs?
column2: RR 28/min, weak rapid radial pulse, BP 88/68 mmHg, pale cool clammy skin; case findings, not universal thresholds.

column1: What indicates hypoperfusion in the chapter's penetrating trauma case despite screaming?
column2: Hypotension, tachypnea, weak rapid peripheral pulse and pale cool clammy skin.

column1: What should an EMT communicate to an ALS partner in the penetrating trauma case?
column2: Serial vital signs, wound locations and changing airway, breathing, bleeding and perfusion findings; do not delay transport for nonessential procedures.

column1: Which structures may neck, anterior chest and abdominal penetrating wounds threaten?
column2: Airway, ventilation, major vessels and internal organs; external location alone does not prove specific injury.

column1: What are BLS priorities for penetrating trauma with hypoperfusion?
column2: Control accessible life-threatening bleeding, manage airway/ventilation, protocol-directed chest injury care, warmth and rapid appropriate trauma transport.

column1: What should be reassessed during transport of a penetrating-trauma patient?
column2: Respiratory effort, bilateral breath sounds, pulse quality, mental status, bleeding and BP; report trends and wound locations.
The body system including the brain, spinal cord, and nerves that controls the voluntary and involuntary activity of the human body.
The brain and the spinal cord (CNS).
The portion of the nervous system located outside the brain and spinal cord (PNS).
Largest part of the brain, responsible for most conscious and sensory functions, the emotions, and the personality.
The section of the brain located beneath the cerebrum that coordinates balance, body movements, and muscle coordination.

The funnel-shaped inferior part of the brain that controls most automatic functions of the body. It is made up of the pons, the midbrain, and the medulla, which is the brain's connection to the spinal cord.
A system of ductless glands that produce hormones that regulate body functions.
The skin.
The outermost layer of the skin.
The second layer of the skin.
A layer of fatty tissue just below the dermis.

column1: What are the four basic nervous-system functions?
column2: Maintain consciousness, transmit sensory information, control motor function and control autonomic body functions.
Three meninges and cushioning cerebrospinal fluid.
Cerebrospinal fluid, cushioning brain and spinal cord.

column1: What is the approximate brain weight in the chapter?
column2: 3 lb.

column1: Why does the brain need constant blood flow?
column2: High oxygen demand and no substantial stored glucose; requires continuous delivery.

column1: What functions are controlled by the cerebrum?
column2: Sensation, thought, speech, memory and conscious movement.

column1: Where is the cerebellum located and what does it do?
column2: Posterior/inferior to cerebrum; coordinates muscle activity and balance.

column1: What are the three brainstem divisions?
column2: Midbrain (mesencephalon), pons and medulla oblongata.

column1: Which centers are located in medulla oblongata?
column2: Respiratory, cardiac and vasomotor centers controlling breathing, heart activity and blood vessel tone.
Specialized barrier permitting selected substances such as glucose to enter brain tissue.

column1: What is the approximate length and function of the spinal cord?
column2: 18 inches; extension of brainstem conducting nerve impulses.
Carry sensory information from body to CNS.
Carry motor information from CNS to body.

column1: Which nerve direction carries a heat sensation to the CNS?
column2: Afferent (sensory).

column1: Which nerve direction activates muscles to withdraw a finger from heat?
column2: Efferent (motor).

column1: What are the two functional nervous system divisions?
column2: Somatic (voluntary) and autonomic (involuntary).

column1: What does the somatic nervous system control?
column2: Skeletal muscles.

column1: What does the autonomic nervous system control?
column2: Automatic function of smooth muscle and glands.

column1: What are the two autonomic divisions?
column2: Sympathetic and parasympathetic.

column1: Which stressors activate the sympathetic nervous system?
column2: Trauma, blood loss and fright.

column1: How does sympathetic activation affect heart and bronchioles?
column2: Raises heart rate and dilates bronchioles.

column1: How does sympathetic activation affect most blood vessels and pupils?
column2: Vasoconstriction and pupil dilation.

column1: How does sympathetic activation affect sweat and digestive secretions?
column2: Increases sweat; decreases saliva and gastric juices.

column1: How does parasympathetic activation affect heart and bronchioles?
column2: Slows heart rate and constricts bronchioles.

column1: How does parasympathetic activation affect pupils and digestive secretions?
column2: Constricts pupils, increases saliva and gastric juices.

column1: How does the chapter describe parasympathetic vascular effects?
column2: Describes dilation of most vessels as opposing sympathetic tone; this is a simplified textbook description, not a universal direct parasympathetic effect.

column1: How does the stress response continue after immediate nerve activation?
column2: Hormonal epinephrine and norepinephrine release sustains it within minutes.
Reticular activating system, brainstem network regulating wakefulness.

column1: What neurologic structures must function for consciousness?
column2: Intact RAS and at least one functioning cerebral hemisphere.

column1: What neurologic dysfunction can cause unconsciousness?
column2: Dysfunction of RAS or both cerebral hemispheres.

column1: Why must an EMT assess airway protection in altered consciousness?
column2: Reduced protective reflexes can allow aspiration; avoid oral intake if swallowing is unsafe.
Chemical messengers released directly into blood by ductless endocrine glands.

column1: Where is the pineal gland and what does it release?
column2: Brain, superior/posterior to thalamus; melatonin.

column1: What functions does melatonin regulate in the chapter?
column2: Circadian rhythm and inhibition of reproductive system (chapter description).

column1: Where is the pituitary gland and why is it called the master gland?
column2: Base of brain; regulates growth and other endocrine glands, metabolism, blood sugar and urinary excretion.

column1: Where is thyroid gland and what does it regulate?
column2: Anterior neck; metabolism, growth, development and nervous-system activity.

column1: Where are parathyroid glands and what do they regulate?
column2: Behind thyroid; calcium and phosphorus metabolism.

column1: Where is thymus and what does it secrete?
column2: Neck/above heart; thymosin for immune development and maturation.

column1: Where are adrenal glands and what are their two parts?
column2: Atop kidneys; cortex and medulla.

column1: What functions are attributed to adrenal glands?
column2: Stress hormones, muscle fatigue delay, sugar storage, kidney function and salt/water regulation.

column1: What are the two major pancreatic hormones?
column2: Insulin and glucagon, from islets of Langerhans.
Facilitates glucose entry into cells.
Raises blood glucose.

column1: Where are gonads and what do they regulate?
column2: Ovaries in lower abdomen and testes in genital region; reproduction and sex characteristics.
Vascular smooth-muscle contraction causes vasoconstriction, reducing skin blood flow and producing pale cool skin.

column1: What primarily mediates sweating in sympathetic activation?
column2: Sympathetic cholinergic fibers, not direct alpha-1 stimulation.
Commonly limits presynaptic norepinephrine release, not release of alpha-1 itself.
Increases heart rate, contraction force and electrical conduction.
Relaxes smooth muscle, especially bronchioles and some vessels.

column1: Which adrenergic receptors does epinephrine activate?
column2: Alpha-1, alpha-2, beta-1 and beta-2.

column1: How does epinephrine counter severe allergic reactions?
column2: Reverses vasodilation and bronchoconstriction; EMT administration only when authorized by local protocol.

column1: Which adrenergic receptor effects predominate with norepinephrine?
column2: Strong alpha effects, meaningful beta-1 activity and relatively little beta-2 effect.

column1: What are the four functions of skin?
column2: Protection, temperature regulation, sensation and water/electrolyte regulation.
Heat, cold, touch, pain and pressure.

column1: What are the three skin layers from superficial to deep?
column2: Epidermis, dermis and subcutaneous layer.

column1: How does the chapter describe epidermal cell layers?
column2: Four layers in its simplified description; outer two dying/dead cells slough off, deepest layers contain melanin.
Pigment in deeper epidermal layers.
Elasticity and strength via dense connective tissue.

column1: Which structures are located in dermis?
column2: Blood vessels, hair follicles/shafts, arrector pili muscles, sweat glands, sebaceous glands and sensory nerves.
Fatty connective tissue, nerves, veins, arteries and sweat glands.

column1: Where is subcutaneous tissue relatively thin versus thick?
column2: Thin on eyelids; thick on abdomen and buttocks.

column1: What are the four accessory skin structures?
column2: Nails, hair, sweat glands and oil glands.

column1: Why can circumferential burns threaten distal circulation?
column2: Edema may constrict circulation; reassess distal pulse, sensation and movement.

column1: What scene safety steps precede approaching the fuel-burn patient?
column2: Park clear of traffic, assess hazards, confirm fire extinguished and fuel/aircraft no longer threaten safety.

column1: What was the patient's initial mental and respiratory status in the fuel-burn case?
column2: Alert, answers appropriately, airway and breathing initially adequate, severe burn pain.

column1: What was the mechanism of the fuel-burn case?
column2: A 38-year-old woman was burned when model airplane fuel ignited during refueling; found about 15 feet from the smoldering aircraft.

column1: What specific airway findings in the burn case raise concern for deterioration?
column2: Oral mucous membrane swelling and singed nasal hair; oral swelling is more direct evidence of airway risk.

column1: Can normal speech or oxygenation initially exclude progressive airway swelling after burns?
column2: No. Reassess voice, breathing, airway and alertness.

column1: How was the right arm injury described anatomically in the fuel-burn case?
column2: Full-thickness burn from right elbow extending inferiorly and circumferentially to distal fingers.

column1: How were head burns described in the fuel-burn case?
column2: Superficial burns involving right cranium and face, lateral right mandible, maxilla and zygomatic arch.

column1: What other secondary assessment findings were documented in the fuel-burn case?
column2: Equal reactive pupils, equal bilateral breath sounds, no dyspnea or other burns, distal pulses present and extremity movement intact.

column1: What were the initial vital-sign trends in the fuel-burn case?
column2: Slightly elevated BP and HR, normal respiratory rate and depth.

column1: What BLS care did the chapter's fuel-burn team provide?
column2: Case-specific oxygen, sterile burn sheets, reassurance and Fowler’s position for comfort/breathing; oxygen decisions depend on findings and exposure.

column1: What did medical direction warn about in the fuel-burn case?
column2: Possible airway compromise from progressive upper airway swelling.

column1: What should be reassessed during transport of the fuel-burn patient?
column2: Mental status, airway, respirations, circulation, vital signs and burn-sheet protection.

column1: What is required at hospital handoff in the fuel-burn case?
column2: Verbal report to ED staff, transfer to bed, PCR with accurate anatomical terms.
Burn through all layers of skin.

column1: Why should an EMT protect burn patients from heat loss?
column2: Skin injury disrupts protective barrier and temperature regulation.
The structures and organs that ingest and carry food so that absorption and waste elimination can occur.
The mechanical and chemical breakdown of food into smaller components that can be absorbed and used by the body.
Passageway at the lower end of the pharynx that leads to the stomach.
The organs and structure responsible for filtering and excreting wastes from the blood.
The male and female organs that function to accomplish human reproduction, the creation of offspring.

column1: What are the two major components of the digestive system?
column2: Alimentary tract and accessory organs.

column1: What are the overall digestive system functions?
column2: Ingest and transport food, digest and absorb nutrients, eliminate waste.

column1: How does digestion start in the mouth?
column2: Mechanical chewing and chemical action of saliva.

column1: Where is the esophagus in relation to the trachea?
column2: Posterior; carries food to stomach.
Hollow organ secreting gastric juices and acid to break down food for absorption.

column1: Where is the pancreas and what are its digestive functions?
column2: Inferior/posterior to stomach; releases juices that digest fats, starches and proteins.

column1: Where is the liver and how large is it relative to other abdominal solid organs?
column2: RUQ beneath diaphragm; largest solid abdominal organ.

column1: What are the major liver functions described?
column2: Produces bile, stores sugars, produces immune/clotting/plasma components and detoxifies substances.
Fat digestion.

column1: Where is the spleen and what does it do?
column2: LUQ solid organ; filters blood, supports immunity and acts as a blood reservoir in the chapter; no digestive function.
Stores bile and contracts to release it into small intestine for fat digestion.

column1: What are the three parts of the small intestine?
column2: Duodenum, jejunum and ileum.

column1: What is the main function of the small intestine?
column2: Completes digestion and absorbs nutrients into bloodstream.

column1: What is the main function of the large intestine?
column2: Absorbs water from remaining waste and forms stool passed through rectum and anus.

column1: What processes make up mechanical digestion?
column2: Chewing, swallowing, peristalsis and defecation (as grouped by chapter).
Rhythmic movement of digestive tract contents.

column1: What does chemical digestion use to break down food?
column2: Enzymes.

column1: What are carbohydrates broken down into in the chapter?
column2: Glucose.

column1: What are fats broken down into in the chapter?
column2: Fatty acids.

column1: What are proteins broken down into?
column2: Amino acids.

column1: What are the functions of the urinary system besides waste removal?
column2: Water/chemical balance, BP regulation, aid RBC production and acid–base balance.

column1: What structures make up the urinary system?
column2: Two kidneys, two ureters, urinary bladder and urethra.

column1: What is the function of the kidneys?
column2: Filter blood and produce urine.
Tube carrying urine from kidney to bladder; two total.
Pelvic organ storing urine.
Tube carrying urine out of the body; anatomy differs between sexes.

column1: Trace urine from production to elimination.
column2: Kidneys → ureters → bladder → urethra.

column1: What is the developmental sequence after fertilization?
column2: Sperm + ovum → fertilized ovum → embryo → fetus → newborn.
Sperm and testosterone.
Stores sperm.
Transports sperm toward urethra.

column1: Which male accessory glands secrete fluid for semen?
column2: Seminal vesicles, bulbourethral gland and prostate gland.

column1: What is the function of the penis in reproduction?
column2: Delivers semen.
Ova, estrogen and progesterone.
Transport ovum toward uterus.

column1: What is the function of uterus?
column2: Site of fetal development.

column1: What are the reproductive functions of vagina?
column2: Receives semen and serves as birth canal.
External female genitalia protecting vaginal opening and urinary meatus.

column1: What is the reproductive function of breasts?
column2: Produce milk.

column1: How does pediatric emergency care compare with adult care?
column2: Similar basic principles, modified for developmental anatomy and physiology.

column1: Why involve caregivers of children with special health care needs?
column2: Individual anatomy, physiology and baseline behavior may differ substantially from typical developmental norms.

column1: Which body system shows the most significant pediatric anatomical differences?
column2: Airway and respiratory system.

column1: How do children's baseline vital signs and blood volume differ from adults?
column2: Faster heart and respiratory rates, lower BP, smaller blood volume and greater dehydration risk.

column1: Does mottling always indicate poor perfusion in a child?
column2: No; cold exposure and immature thermoregulation can also cause mottling.

column1: How do pediatric tracheal and esophageal openings differ from adults?
column2: They are closer together.

column1: Why is a child's proportionally large tongue important?
column2: Can easily obstruct airway with altered consciousness; small oral cavity leaves little room for swelling.

column1: What is the newborn tracheal diameter compared with adult diameter?
column2: Approximately 4–5 mm versus 20 mm in adults.

column1: Why can airway inflammation become critical more quickly in children?
column2: A small amount of swelling severely narrows the already smaller airway.

column1: How do pediatric tracheal rings and cricoid cartilage differ from adults?
column2: More pliable, underdeveloped rings except first ring, and less rigid cricoid.

column1: Why avoid hyperflexion and hyperextension of an infant's neck?
column2: Soft airway structures may partially or completely occlude.

column1: What padding may help maintain pediatric airway alignment?
column2: A folded towel approximately 1 inch thick under shoulders may help; adjust to child and neutral alignment.

column1: Why avoid pressure on soft tissue under a child's chin during airway maneuvers?
column2: It can push tongue backward into pharynx and obstruct airway.

column1: Are infants invariably obligate nasal breathers?
column2: No; they strongly prefer nasal breathing and may not automatically compensate for nasal obstruction, but oral breathing is possible.

column1: Why may nasal congestion rapidly cause infant respiratory distress?
column2: Infants strongly prefer nasal breathing; secretions, blood or inflammation may obstruct their small nasal passages.

column1: What is the traditional textbook claim about the narrowest pediatric airway segment?
column2: Cricoid cartilage until about age 6; debated, since imaging identifies narrower glottic dimensions. Maintain alignment and avoid soft-tissue compression rather than relying on this rule.

column1: How does the pediatric epiglottis differ from the adult epiglottis?
column2: Higher in airway; chapter associates this with greater aspiration risk especially during hyperextension.

column1: Why are children more prone to head injury during falls and crashes?
column2: Head is proportionally larger.

column1: How does a child's large occiput affect alignment when supine?
column2: It pushes head forward and flexes neck on a flat surface.

column1: How can an EMT maintain neutral pediatric airway/spinal alignment?
column2: Place appropriate padding behind shoulders to compensate for large occiput; individualize and avoid forced alignment.

column1: Until approximately what age may children need shoulder padding according to the chapter?
column2: 8–9 years; adult proportions by approximately age 10. Individualize padding.

column1: At what age do infants typically begin to support their own head in the chapter?
column2: Younger than 6–7 months may not fully support head; support the head when lifting a baby.
Soft spot due to incomplete closure of skull plates; do not press or poke it.

column1: When does anterior fontanelle typically close?
column2: 12–18 months in the chapter.

column1: When does posterior fontanelle typically close?
column2: By 3 months in the chapter.

column1: Why should an EMT not rely on fontanelle appearance alone?
column2: Sunken/bulging assessment is difficult and unreliable prehospital.

column1: What is more important than a bulging fontanelle when assessing possible increased ICP?
column2: Decreased mental status.

column1: Why can an infant with unfused skull plates still develop brain compression?
column2: Acute swelling over hours to days cannot be accommodated by dura.

column1: Which findings are more useful than sunken fontanelle for dehydration?
column2: Tachycardia, mottling, caregiver report of fewer tears and wet diapers.

column1: Why can a child sustain internal chest injury without rib fracture?
column2: Pliable ribs deform rather than break and protect internal organs less effectively.

column1: Why do infants depend heavily on diaphragm for breathing?
column2: Horizontal ribs have poor leverage to expand chest; chest muscles are underdeveloped.

column1: Which lung injuries are pediatric patients particularly susceptible to?
column2: Pulmonary contusion after blunt trauma and pneumothorax with excessive positive pressure ventilation.

column1: Is abdominal rise during infant inhalation normal?
column2: Yes; pliable immature ribs cause little chest movement; abdomen normally rises on inhalation and falls on exhalation.

column1: Which retractions are described with mild pediatric respiratory distress?
column2: Intercostal retractions, between ribs.

column1: Which retractions suggest more severe pediatric respiratory distress?
column2: Suprasternal, supraclavicular and sternal retractions.

column1: Why are infant lungs prone to collapse?
column2: Compliant chest wall, small airways and dependence on diaphragm.
Closing vocal cords and bearing down abdominally at end of inspiration to maintain positive pressure and prevent collapse; exhausting.

column1: Does pediatric RR of 60/min necessarily indicate inadequate breathing?
column2: No. Textbook threshold is not universal; normal infants can breathe near 60/min. Assess appearance, effort, air movement, color and oxygenation.

column1: What does a declining respiratory rate in an exhausted child suggest?
column2: Possible respiratory failure; not necessarily improvement.

column1: What does a caregiver report of brief apnea and cyanosis in an infant indicate?
column2: Concerning episode; prompt assessment and rapid transport.

column1: How does baseline breathing in children under age 5 compare to adults in the chapter?
column2: 2–3 times faster, shallower, requiring smaller volume and pressure for ventilation.

column1: Why can respiratory effort itself worsen an infant's illness?
column2: Diaphragm fatigues easily and respiratory work consumes oxygen needed by other organs.

column1: What does a lethargic infant with loss of normal behavior or attitude suggest?
column2: Severe illness, particularly if working hard to breathe; urgent intervention and transport/advanced care.

column1: Which factors increase pediatric heart rate?
column2: Fear, fever, anxiety, hypoxia, activity and hypovolemia.

column1: How does pediatric bradycardia relate to hypoxia?
column2: Chapter describes it as late response in infants/children and initial response in newborns; severe hypoxia can cause bradycardia, requiring prompt oxygenation/ventilation assessment.

column1: Why is even a small hemorrhage serious in a child?
column2: Smaller circulating blood volume; promptly control bleeding.

column1: At approximately what blood loss does the chapter describe pediatric hypotension developing?
column2: Usually after greater than 30% blood volume lost; approximation, not threshold for treatment. Hypotension can occur suddenly as compensation fails.

column1: Why is a normal BP not reassuring in suspected pediatric shock?
column2: Children may maintain pressure until advanced shock; assess perfusion and serial findings.

column1: How do infants and young children primarily compensate for reduced cardiac output?
column2: Increase heart rate and peripheral vasoconstriction, with limited ability to increase cardiac contractility.

column1: Which skin findings may reflect pediatric compensatory vasoconstriction?
column2: Cool extremities and mottling; interpret alongside temperature and other findings.

column1: What determines BP in pediatric circulation?
column2: Cardiac output and systemic vascular resistance.

column1: Why is blunt abdominal trauma especially concerning in children?
column2: Underdeveloped abdominal muscles offer less protection to organs.

column1: Until when are liver and spleen relatively exposed in children?
column2: Until puberty, they are less protected by ribs.
Pediatric bone bends and splinters rather than breaking completely through.

column1: How does pediatric motor development progress?
column2: From head toward toes; immature coordination contributes to falls.

column1: How much faster do children's cells use oxygen and glucose in the chapter?
column2: 2–3 times faster than adult cells, even at rest.

column1: Why do apnea, hypoventilation and poor oxygenation cause faster pediatric CNS injury?
column2: Higher metabolic oxygen and glucose demand.

column1: Why may children show signs of CO poisoning sooner than adults?
column2: Higher metabolic rate and oxygen demand.

column1: What are the four factors predisposing children to acute hypoglycemia?
column2: Poor glucose stores, immature liver glucose release, high metabolic demand and diabetes history.

column1: Which findings may indicate pediatric hypoglycemia?
column2: Twitching, seizures, limpness, eye rolling, apnea or irregular respirations.

column1: Why does pediatric hypoglycemia require rapid recognition and intervention?
column2: Onset can be rapid and cause cerebral injury; assess and treat per protocol.
When the patient cannot swallow safely; follow authorized glucose assessment/treatment protocols.

column1: Why does a large BSA-to-mass ratio predispose children to hypothermia?
column2: Relatively large surface area increases heat loss; protect against environmental extremes.
Body surface area.

column1: Which skin and neurologic characteristics impair pediatric thermoregulation?
column2: Thin delicate skin, less subcutaneous tissue and immature hypothalamus, especially newborns.

column1: What age group does the geriatric demographics section discuss?
column2: Adults aged 65 and older.

column1: Which U.S. age group does the chapter describe as the fastest-growing population segment?
column2: Adults over age 65; historical textbook characterization, not an independently verified current demographic claim.

column1: What was the chapter's historical 2019 U.S. older-adult population estimate?
column2: 54.1 million people aged 65+, about 16% of population; historical figure.

column1: What was the chapter's projection for U.S. older-adult population in 2040?
column2: 81 million, about 22% of population; textbook projection, not current estimate.

column1: What EMS call-volume projection does the chapter give for 2030?
column2: More than 50% of EMS calls involving elderly patients; textbook projection, not verified current forecast.

column1: Why can geriatric emergencies present differently from younger adults?
column2: Normal physiological changes, chronic comorbidities and medications may mask or change symptoms.
Use of multiple medications; can alter clinical presentation and raise medication-related risks.

column1: At what approximate age does normal physiologic aging begin in the chapter?
column2: Around age 30; lifestyle and healthcare may slow but not stop it.

column1: How do chronic and acute illnesses differ?
column2: Chronic is long-term/gradual; acute has rapid onset and may be severe.

column1: Why do older adults tolerate acute illness and trauma less well?
column2: Reduced physiologic reserve limits compensation.

column1: Is illness an inevitable part of normal aging?
column2: No; normal aging is not itself disease, but disease or injury can worsen age-related changes.

column1: Why might infection be less apparent in older patients?
column2: Reduced immune defenses and fever may be absent.

column1: Should acute confusion be attributed to normal aging or dementia without assessment?
column2: No; assess acute change and compare baseline function.
Narrowing of a valve opening restricting blood flow and ability to meet increased demands.

column1: How can calcium deposits affect aging heart valves?
column2: Contribute to deterioration and narrowing of valve openings.
Backward flow when a valve fails to seal.

column1: Which valve is more commonly associated with regurgitation in the chapter?
column2: Mitral (bicuspid) rather than tricuspid.

column1: How can mitral regurgitation cause pulmonary edema?
column2: Blood backs up into left atrium and pulmonary circulation.

column1: How does age-related cardiac wall thickening reduce reserve in the chapter?
column2: Fibrous tissue replacement and thickening without chamber enlargement reduce stroke volume and cardiac output.
Blood ejected per heartbeat.
Blood ejected per minute.

column1: How does aging affect the heart rate response to stress?
column2: Fewer conducting cells and reduced catecholamine responsiveness limit the increase in heart rate; older adults do not universally have higher resting rates.

column1: Why can an older patient in shock lack marked tachycardia?
column2: Reduced cardiac responsiveness, conduction disease or medications can blunt rate response.
Irregular myocardial contraction associated with electrical disturbance; can be critical or fatal.

column1: How can aging cardiac conduction changes affect pulse findings?
column2: Impaired impulse initiation/propagation may produce weak, irregular or absent pulse.
Hardening and loss of arterial elasticity, increasing resistance and systolic BP in the chapter.

column1: Where are the pressure sensors described in geriatric BP regulation?
column2: Aortic arch and carotid region; signal brainstem.

column1: Why does decreased baroreceptor sensitivity predispose older adults to orthostatic hypotension?
column2: Impaired BP regulation when changing position.
BP falls on moving from lying to standing; chapter describes possible accompanying HR increase. Do not provoke standing in unstable or fall-prone patients.

column1: How does aging affect chest-wall flexibility?
column2: Respiratory muscles weaken and calcium deposits at rib-sternum joints stiffen chest wall.

column1: Until what age does the chapter describe new alveoli being generated?
column2: Around age 20, a textbook teaching figure.

column1: How does loss of alveolar surface area affect older adults?
column2: Reduces oxygen and CO₂ diffusion capacity.

column1: Where are the chemoreceptors described in the chapter?
column2: Aortic arch, carotid bodies and brainstem surface.

column1: How does diminished chemoreceptor sensitivity affect older patients?
column2: Reduced responsiveness to hypoxia and hypercapnia.
Low oxygen availability.
Elevated carbon dioxide.

column1: How do aging bronchiolar changes affect airflow?
column2: Fewer/weaker supporting smooth muscle fibers, turbulent airflow, less air reaches terminal alveoli and air trapping on exhalation.

column1: At what age does airflow velocity start declining in the chapter?
column2: After age 30; COPD, stress, shock or pneumonia may worsen decline.

column1: Why are older adults more vulnerable to pneumonia?
column2: Weaker cough reflex, reduced ciliary clearance and protective airway antibodies, plus common dehydration.

column1: How does oxygenation differ from ventilation in geriatric respiratory care?
column2: Oxygen alone does not correct inadequate ventilation; assess and support ventilation when indicated.

column1: How does aging affect brain mass and CSF volume?
column2: Decreased brain mass and weight leave more space filled by CSF.

column1: What do the chapter's age-related neuronal plaques and tangles represent?
column2: Abnormal accumulation of waste products associated with impaired brain function; not universal proof of disease.

column1: When does the chapter describe neuronal degeneration beginning?
column2: As early as mid-20s.

column1: Why do age-related neurologic changes increase fall risk?
column2: Slowed reflexes, impaired position sense and unsteadiness combine with muscle/joint changes.

column1: Which regulatory functions may decline with age?
column2: Hunger/thirst perception, breathing rate/depth, HR, BP and core temperature regulation during stress.

column1: Which senses may diminish in older adults?
column2: Hearing, vision, smell, touch, pain, hot/cold and body position sense.
Clarity of vision; often decreases with age.
Ability to focus at varying distances; often decreases with age.

column1: Which other visual changes occur with aging?
column2: Reduced color discrimination, night/dark vision and tear production, sometimes causing irritation.

column1: How do age-related visual changes affect safety?
column2: Increased falls and medication dosage errors; combined hearing and visual loss also increases crash/injury risk.
Clouding of lens obstructing light reaching retina.
Optic nerve damage associated with intraocular pressure; chapter calls it second leading cause of blindness in U.S., an unverified textbook ranking.
Loss of central vision, impairing reading and face recognition; peripheral vision may remain.
Separation of retina from supportive tissue, causing local or complete visual loss.
Progressive bilateral symmetrical age-related hearing loss, most marked at high frequencies; trouble distinguishing speech from background noise.

column1: How should an EMT communicate with a patient with presbycusis?
column2: Verify hearing aid is worn and on; avoid shouting because it distorts sound.
Abnormal function of motor, sensory or autonomic nerve tracts.

column1: How do diffuse and focal neuropathy differ?
column2: Diffuse affects many nerve tracts; focal affects a single nerve.
Pain, numbness, tingling, swelling, weakness or absent pain perception.

column1: Why can neuropathy conceal myocardial infarction in diabetic patients?
column2: Reduced pain perception may cause silent MI without chest pain.

column1: Which areas are commonly affected by diabetic peripheral neuropathy in the chapter?
column2: Hands and feet.

column1: How do reduced taste and smell contribute to malnutrition in older adults?
column2: Reduced food enjoyment may lead to irregular eating.

column1: How can aging affect oral intake and swallowing?
column2: Impaired swallowing, periodontal disease, gum/tooth loss and reduced saliva.

column1: Why does chronic heartburn become more common with aging?
column2: Reduced esophageal smooth-muscle contraction and reduced tone between esophagus and stomach allow reflux.

column1: How does reduced gastric hydrochloric acid affect digestion?
column2: Less efficient breakdown of food.

column1: How does aging affect liver structure and function?
column2: Reduced size, weight, enzymes and blood flow impair digestion and drug metabolism.

column1: How does aging affect GI peristalsis?
column2: Slows throughout GI tract.

column1: Why may aging small intestine contribute to malnutrition?
column2: Degeneration of lining impairs nutrient absorption.

column1: Why may older adults develop constipation or fecal impaction?
column2: Reduced large intestine contractions.

column1: Why may bowel control decline with age?
column2: Degeneration of rectal sphincter muscle.

column1: How does aging insulin responsiveness affect glucose?
column2: Reduced effectiveness/receptor response, mild carbohydrate intolerance and increased type 2 diabetes risk.

column1: Which vasopressor hormones does the chapter associate with age-related hypertension?
column2: Norepinephrine and vasopressin.

column1: Which hormone changes can impair fluid and BP regulation in older adults?
column2: Altered renin and aldosterone, increased atrial natriuretic hormone (ANH), contributing to retention or dehydration and BP changes.
Atrial natriuretic hormone released by atrial muscle; participates in water and sodium regulation.

column1: How does reduced beta stimulation responsiveness affect older patients?
column2: Reduced heart and vascular smooth-muscle response, contributing to BP regulation problems including hypertension and orthostatic hypotension.

column1: How does aging affect thyroid hormones in the chapter?
column2: Reduced thyroxine metabolism and conversion to triiodothyronine, affecting temperature, growth and heart rate.

column1: Which joint disease is described as common in older patients?
column2: Osteoarthritis.
Loss of bone minerals leading to brittle bones, higher fracture risk and slower healing.

column1: Why can fractures and immobility be especially dangerous in older adults?
column2: Delayed healing and immobility may lead to further illness or death.
Spinal curvature associated in the chapter with narrowed intervertebral disks, most prominent in thoracic spine.

column1: How common is kyphosis according to the chapter?
column2: Approximately two of three elderly patients; textbook estimate.

column1: How should SMR be adapted for geriatric kyphosis?
column2: Respect baseline curvature, pad voids and use approved transport equipment; never force flat alignment. Backboard may assist extrication but is not routinely needed for ongoing transport.

column1: How do aging articular cartilage, synovial fluid and ligaments affect joints?
column2: Cartilage thins, fluid thickens and ligaments weaken, reducing range of motion and increasing pain and injury risk.

column1: How does loss of skeletal muscle mass affect older patients?
column2: Weakness, impaired balance, falls and slow-healing fractures.

column1: What age-related kidney structural change reduces filtration surface?
column2: Loss of nephrons; chapter estimates kidney weight declines by about one-third.

column1: How do cardiovascular changes impair renal filtration?
column2: Reduced renal blood flow means less blood filtered per minute.
Fluid and electrolyte imbalances.

column1: Why are older adults more vulnerable to drug toxicity?
column2: Reduced liver metabolism and renal filtration can cause drug accumulation with excess or frequent dosing.

column1: Why may acute illness cause renal failure despite acceptable baseline kidney function?
column2: Reduced renal reserve cannot meet additional demands.

column1: What are geriatric toxicologic emergency risk factors in the chapter?
column2: Reduced kidney/liver function, altered GI absorption, poor eyesight/motor skills, medication noncompliance, polypharmacy and reduced blood–brain barrier integrity.

column1: Why should an EMT obtain a medication history in an older adult?
column2: Multiple medications and reduced clearance may mask illness or increase toxicity; note baseline function and recent doses.

column1: Why does aging skin become thinner?
column2: Deterioration of subcutaneous tissue and reduced attachment between dermis and epidermis.

column1: Why do older patients heal skin wounds slowly?
column2: Slower cell replacement and regeneration.

column1: How does aging affect perspiration and sensation?
column2: Less perspiration and dulled touch sensation.

column1: Why are older patients prone to sores, skin tears and infection?
column2: Fragile skin and weakened protective barrier.
Increased risk of hypothermia and hyperthermia.

column1: What precautions help protect older patients' fragile skin?
column2: Minimize unnecessary exposure, pad pressure points and protect skin during movement.
